The inner product on \mathbb {R}^{m\times n}, obtained by treating a matrix as a long vector and summing the entrywise products: \langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle \ :=\ \sum _{i=1}^{m}\sum _{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}Z_{ij}, the direct generalization of the vector case \langle \mathbf {x},\mathbf {z}\rangle =\sum _i x_i z_i. It is the inner product whose induced norm is the Frobenius norm, \|\mathbf {X}\|_F=\sqrt {\langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {X}\rangle }.
It has a compact trace form (see Matrix trace): \langle \mathbf {X},\mathbf {Z}\rangle \ =\ \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}^{\top }\mathbf {Z})\ =\ \mathrm {tr}(\mathbf {X}\mathbf {Z}^{\top }).

A page table that is itself paged: instead of one linear array of PTEs, the table is split into page-sized chunks indexed by a top-level page directory. Subtrees of the address space that are entirely unused get a single null entry at the top level — no second-level page is allocated for them. This is the design that displaced Segmented page tables — it preserves the "don't pay for empty regions" property while keeping every piece of the structure page-sized, eliminating the variable-allocation fragmentation that doomed the segmented version.
Advantages over a linear Page table:

html:ol.html:li: Fits easily in memory — only allocate a second-level page when an entry in it is used.
Memory cost is proportional to the amount of address space actually in use.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. On a Translation lookaside buffer miss, the walk now costs two memory loads — page directory entry first, then the PTE.
Remark. Real architectures push this further (x86-64 uses 4 or 5 levels) and lean on the TLB to absorb the walk cost.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The information-theoretic reading of a Markov chain: three variables form a chain U\to V\to W when W depends on U only through V, P(W=w\mid U=u, V=v)\ =\ P(W=w\mid V=v). Equivalently, U and W are conditionally independent given V, written (U\perp W)\mid V: P(U=u, W=w\mid V=v)\ =\ P(U=u\mid V=v)\,P(W=w\mid V=v).

Two consequences make this the right object for information theory. The relation is reversible — U\to V\to W \iff W\to V\to U — because conditional independence is symmetric in U and W. And any estimator forms a chain X\to Y\to \hat X: an estimate \hat X is computed from the observation Y alone, never touching X directly. That structure is exactly what the data processing inequality needs — you cannot manufacture information about X by processing Y.
Let f:\mathbb {R}^n\to \mathbb {R} be twice continuously differentiable in an open neighborhood of \mathbf {x_\star }.

Necessary. If \mathbf {x_\star } is a local minimizer, then (i)\ \nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })=\mathbf {0};\qquad (ii)\ \nabla ^2 f(\mathbf {x_\star })\succeq \mathbf {0}. That is, it is a stationary point whose Hessian is positive semidefinite.

Sufficient. If instead \nabla f(\mathbf {x_\star })=\mathbf {0} and \nabla ^2 f(\mathbf {x_\star })\succ \mathbf {0} (Hessian strictly positive definite), then \mathbf {x_\star } is a strict local minimizer. The gap between \succeq and \succ is exactly the ambiguity the first-order condition alone cannot resolve.

fr:title.text: Memory coalescing merges a warp's accesses into one transaction per cache line

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Memory coalescing merges a warp's accesses into one transaction per cache line

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The hardware optimization on GPUs that combines simultaneous memory accesses by threads in a warp into a single transaction — when the accessed addresses fall in the same cache line.
Global memory latency on a GPU is 400–800 cycles. Coalescing is the primary way to keep the SM fed:

html:ul.html:li: If all 32 threads in a warp access addresses within one cache line: one memory transaction, full bandwidth.
If addresses span multiple cache lines: the hardware serializes into multiple transactions; bandwidth drops proportionally.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Address permutations within a cache line don't hurt utilization — coalescing is about which lines are touched, not which exact bytes.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Coalescing is why memory layout matters so much for GPU code. The standard idiom is structure-of-arrays (SoA) instead of array-of-structures (AoS): threads accessing the same field of consecutive records hit consecutive bytes, which coalesce; threads accessing the same struct don't.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. Should you always cache on the GPU?

html:div.html:details: Answer.No. If you're memory-bound and have no Spatial locality, cache is wasted on data you won't reuse. CUDA exposes the option to disable L1 caching for these cases, which lets misaligned loads transfer only the bytes needed instead of full cache lines.

This is the mirror image of KL divergence is jointly convex. Writing H(P)=\log |\mathcal {X}|-D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\,\|\,U) against the uniform law U, concavity of H is exactly convexity of P\mapsto D_{\mathrm {KL}}(P\|U). Concavity is what makes the maximum in The uniform distribution maximizes entropy well-behaved — a concave objective on the simplex has a unique maximizer.
For any pair of random variables, I(X;Y)\geq 0, with equality iff X and Y are independent.

This is Gibb's inequality in disguise: mutual information is the KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals, I(X;Y)\ =\ D_{\mathrm {KL}}\left (P_{XY}\,\|\,P_X P_Y\right )\ \geq \ 0, and Gibbs' inequality forces every KL divergence to be nonnegative, vanishing exactly when the two arguments coincide — i.e. when P_{XY}=P_XP_Y. It is the root fact from which Conditioning reduces entropy follows.

fr:title.text: Warp divergence serializes both sides of a branch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Warp divergence serializes both sides of a branch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: When threads in a warp take different branches of a conditional, the warp does not split into smaller warps. Instead, the active mask selects which lanes execute each branch; lanes on the inactive side run dummy instructions until the warp reconverges at the post-conditional join point. The programmer writes ordinary scalar code with if/else, and the hardware silently masks the inactive lanes.

This is the chief ergonomic win over SIMD: the compiler does not have to prove that all lanes will take the same path. The cost is that divergent code pays for both sides — a 32-wide warp where 16 threads take the if-branch and 16 take the else-branch executes both branches sequentially with half the lanes idle each time.

The hardware sequences the two paths with a reconvergence stack — or, on recent GPUs, a barrier-based equivalent that avoids its deadlocks. The standard software mitigation is Warp Specialization: group threads with the same control-flow trajectory into one warp so the branch never diverges in the first place.

fr:title.text: A reconvergence stack sequences a warp's divergent paths and can deadlock

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A reconvergence stack sequences a warp's divergent paths and can deadlock

fr:mainmatter.html:p: When a warp diverges, the hardware needs to remember where the split paths rejoin. The classical mechanism is a reconvergence stack: each entry holds a next-PC, a reconvergence PC (the post-conditional join point), and an active mask. On a divergent branch the hardware pushes both sides and executes them one at a time, popping back to the reconvergence point as each side completes; entries are pushed largest-mask-first to bound stack depth.

The stack has a fatal flaw. A thread that exits a loop diverges and is stacked below threads still spinning inside it — so if those spinning threads wait on a lock the exited thread already holds, neither can proceed and the program deadlocks. This is why modern NVIDIA hardware abandons the stack for a barrier-based scheme: each divergence point is tracked by a 32-bit participation mask, letting the scheduler switch between branches arbitrarily and guarantee independent thread progress.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Murphi is an explicit-state model checker: you describe a system as guarded transition rules, state the invariants, and it enumerates every reachable interleaving looking for a violation. That makes it a natural fit for cache coherence, where the steady-state behavior is easy and the races are not. This post builds a directory-based MESI protocol in Murphi, starting from MSI and adding state every time the checker finds a way to break it.

The state tables come from A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, which doubles as the source for these notes. The recurring lesson is that the published tables are not quite enough: every protocol below needs transient states the tables leave implicit.

A rule is a transition from one state to another

html:ul.html:li: Each rule can optionally have an initial condition required to be fired
We can easily define rules for all the processors or collection of n things with ruleset.
For our use case, rules are used to define

html:ol.html:li: Receiving a request from the network

An invariant is something that Murphi checks to ensure is true at all possible configurations of the system.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The valid-invalid protocol shipped with the Murphi docs uses two Virtual Channels. A directory protocol needs three: one each for requests, forwarded requests, and responses. The reason is that deadlock is a cycle in the dependency graph, so it suffices to exhibit one.

html:ul.html:li: A node issues GetS to the directory, giving an edge N_1 \to D.
The directory forwards Fwd-GetS to the owner, extending the chain to N_1 \to D \to N_2.
The owner sends data back to the requester, closing the cycle N_1 \to D \to N_2 \to N_1.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The data closing that cycle would travel on the same channel as the requests waiting behind it, so a full request buffer wedges the response that would drain it. Partitioning by message class breaks the cycle:

html:ul.html:li: Request: GetS, GetM, PutS, PutM
Forwarded: Fwd-GetS, Fwd-GetM, Inv, PutAck
Response: Data, InvAck

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are enumerated directly in the model's MessageType.

fr:title.text: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Consider the PutM rule that downgrades a cache from modified to invalid. The evicting cache must not drop the data when it sends PutM, because it may still have to service a forwarded request; it transitions to MI^A and keeps the value. But nothing stops the PutAck from arriving first, taking it to I before the Fwd-GetM shows up. The data is gone and the forwarded request has nobody to answer it.

Fix. Add the M^D state to the directory controller. While in M^D, a PutM from a node that is not the current owner stalls until the data arrives. Leaving M^D for M requires the new owner to send data back to the directory even on a three-hop transaction, so the directory learns that the forward actually completed. I have not found a cleaner way to close this race without the extra state.

fr:title.text: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The M^D fix introduces a deadlock of its own. Take two processors that store-miss and a third that load-misses. The second store wins at the directory: the first store gets data and moves IM^{AD} \to IM^{A}, then the second triggers a Fwd-GetM that takes ownership away from it.

Meanwhile the load miss sits in IS^D. When its Inv arrives, the table says to stall — and because Inv and Fwd-GetM share the forwarded channel, that stall blocks the Fwd-GetM behind it. The winning processor never receives the data, and nothing ever drains the channel.

Fix. Another transient state absent from the table: II^A, meaning "was in IS^A, got invalidated, now waiting on PutAck before settling in I". The invalidation is processed rather than stalled, so the forwarded channel keeps moving.

fr:title.text: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One more correction to the table: when the home directory is in M and receives a GetS, it must not clear the owner field as the figure directs. Once in S^D, the directory can no longer tell whether an incoming PutM came from the owner (and should stall) or from a stale node. The owner is only cleared once the data has actually arrived.

html:figure.html:figcaption: MESI directory controller, evictions and data. A PutM carries the line with it; a PutE never does, since E is clean, which is why only the PutM column writes back.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Symmetrically, the directory gains an E^D state, which for completeness is kept distinct from M^D but could be folded into it.

The first processor issues GetS and waits in IS^D, while the home directory has already moved to E and sent it ExclusiveData. A second processor then issues GetM, and home's Fwd-GetM overtakes the data in flight.
Fix. Stall Fwd-GetM and Fwd-GetS in IS^D until the data lands. This is safe here because the data is on the response channel, which no stall can block.

fr:title.text: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The nastier version of the same race: the invalidation arrives before the forward. By the II^A rule inherited from MSI, a PutAck in that state drops the line to I. This discards data a forwarded request is about to ask for.

html:ol.html:li: Home takes the first GetS from Proc_1 → E, sends ExclusiveData
Proc_1 receives ExclusiveData → I, and the data is lost

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix. ExclusiveData pays for itself a second time. Because the message is distinguishable from ordinary Data, a cache receiving it in II^D knows it was the first reader and transitions to E instead of I. There, the pending Fwd-GetM or Fwd-GetS is handled correctly.
Folding all of the above in leaves these two state machines, which Murphi verifies exhaustively.
